title: Performance in Frameworks
summary: Memoization and list virtualization are the two levers that matter once a UI gets big enough to feel slow — but both are measured fixes, not defaults, and the profiler is what tells you which one, if either, actually applies.

slides.markdown:
Every performance topic before this one in the group has been about **correctness that happens to also affect performance** — a stable `key`, deriving instead of storing, splitting a Context. This topic is about the tools you reach for once correctness is solid and something is still measurably slow: **memoization** (skip re-rendering or recomputing work that didn't need to happen) and **virtualization** (skip rendering DOM nodes that aren't visible).

The recurring interview trap here isn't knowing the APIs — it's applying them without measuring first. Every framework's advanced-performance question ends the same way: "this list is janky when scrolling — diagnose and fix it," and the strong answers all start with the profiler, not with sprinkling `memo` everywhere and hoping.

A component re-renders for exactly one of three reasons: **its own state changed**, **its props changed**, or **its parent re-rendered** (and this component isn't memoized, so React re-renders it too even if its own props are identical to last time).

That third reason is the one people underestimate. In React's default model, a parent re-rendering re-renders every non-memoized child **unconditionally** — not because the child's props actually differ, but because React doesn't know they don't unless something tells it to check. A component with props that are always the literal same values can still re-render dozens of times if its parent re-renders often, purely as a side effect of sitting in that subtree.

This is the mechanism that makes an unrelated state update elsewhere in a large tree feel like it's "causing" slowness in a component that never actually changed — it's not the component's own logic, it's an unmemoized subtree re-rendering along with its parent.

slides.sectionTitle: React.memo, useMemo, useCallback — what each memoizes
slides.markdown:
Three related but distinct tools, frequently confused for one another:

- **`React.memo(Component)`** memoizes a **component**: it skips re-rendering the wrapped component if its props are shallow-equal to last time, even when its parent re-renders.
- **`useMemo(fn, deps)`** memoizes a **computed value**: it re-runs `fn` only when a dependency changes, returning the cached result otherwise — for an expensive calculation, not for a component.
- **`useCallback(fn, deps)`** memoizes a **function reference**: it returns the same function identity across renders as long as dependencies haven't changed — its entire purpose is making `React.memo` on a child actually work when that child receives a callback prop, since a new function reference every render would otherwise defeat the shallow-equality check.

The three are usually used together, not individually: `useCallback` stabilizes a function prop, so that a child wrapped in `React.memo` can actually see "same props as last time" and skip its own re-render.

slides.sectionTitle: List virtualization: render only visible rows
slides.markdown:
Rendering a list of 10,000 rows means creating 10,000 real DOM nodes, even though a typical viewport only shows 15–20 of them at once — the other ~9,980 are pure waste: memory, layout cost, and paint cost for pixels no one can see.

**Virtualization** (also called "windowing") renders only the rows currently in or near the visible viewport, plus a small buffer, and swaps their content as the user scrolls rather than creating a DOM node per data item. The scrollable area is given the *correct total height* as if all 10,000 rows existed (so the scrollbar behaves normally), but the actual DOM at any moment holds only the handful of rows near the viewport — repositioned and re-populated with new data as scroll position changes.

The trade-off: virtualization adds real complexity — variable row heights, keyboard navigation, and browser find-in-page all get harder when most of the list literally doesn't exist in the DOM at any given moment — so it's a tool for lists that are actually long enough to need it, not a default for every list.

slides.sectionTitle: Memoizing everything, with no measured gain
slides.markdown:
`React.memo`/`useMemo`/`useCallback` are not free. Each one adds a comparison step (shallow-equality checks on every render) and a small amount of memory to hold the cached value or function — wrapping a component or value that re-renders cheaply and rarely benefits from being skipped can make things **slightly slower**, not faster, while definitely making the code harder to read.

The overuse pattern looks like wrapping every single component in `memo` and every inline function in `useCallback` reflexively, "because performance." This has a real readability cost — dependency arrays to maintain, and a new failure mode where a missing dependency in `useCallback`/`useMemo` causes the exact same stale-closure bugs covered in the hooks topic — for wins that were never measured and, for a component that renders in under a millisecond regardless, are often literally unmeasurable.

The rule that actually holds up: memoize where a profiler has shown a real cost, not preemptively across the whole codebase.

slides.sectionTitle: Using the profiler to find the actual bottleneck
slides.markdown:
Every mainstream framework ships (or has a widely-used extension providing) a devtools profiler that records **which components rendered, how long each took, and why** — React DevTools' Profiler tab, Vue Devtools' performance panel, and browser-native Performance panels all serve this role.

The workflow that actually finds the bottleneck: record a profile while performing the slow interaction (typing in a search box, scrolling a list), then look at two things — which components rendered far more often than expected, and which single component's render actually took the most wall-clock time. Those are frequently **different** components: a component re-rendering 200 times but each render taking 0.1ms is not your bottleneck; a component rendering twice but taking 40ms each time almost certainly is.

The profiler also often reveals the *actual* cause is something other than rendering at all — a synchronous computation inside the render body, an unmemoized expensive `.filter()`/`.sort()` call, or (outside the framework's control entirely) layout thrashing from reading a DOM measurement and writing a style in alternating order.

| | React | Vue 3 | Svelte |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Manual re-render skip** | `React.memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` | rarely needed — fine-grained reactivity already skips unaffected subtrees | rarely needed — compiled reactivity updates only the affected DOM directly |
| **List virtualization** | `react-window`, `TanStack Virtual` (userland libraries) | `vue-virtual-scroller`, `TanStack Virtual` | `svelte-virtual-list`, `TanStack Virtual` |

The manual-memoization row is the direct consequence of the reactivity-model topic earlier in this group: React needs explicit opt-outs *because* it doesn't track dependencies, while Vue and Svelte's fine-grained tracking already knows what depends on what, so there's usually nothing to manually skip. Virtualization, by contrast, is needed in every framework equally — it's about DOM node count, which no reactivity model changes; all three ecosystems rely on largely the same userland libraries to solve it.

slides.sectionTitle: When memoization itself becomes the bottleneck
slides.markdown:
A senior-level nuance beyond "measure before memoizing": memoization has diminishing, sometimes negative, returns as **dependency array size and comparison cost grow.** A `useMemo` with a deep object as a dependency, compared by reference on every render, is cheap. A component wrapped in `React.memo` that receives a dozen props, each requiring its own shallow-equality check, pays a real per-render cost for the check itself — and if most of those props actually do change nearly every render anyway, the memoization never pays off; it's pure overhead on top of a re-render that was going to happen regardless.

This is why blanket "wrap every component in memo" advice breaks down at scale: the right targets are components that are both **expensive to render** and **re-render with unchanged props reasonably often** — not every component in the tree indiscriminately. Profiling for exactly this pair of conditions, rather than assuming either one implies the other, is what separates a measured optimization from cargo-cult memoization.

This is one of the most common practical performance questions, and a strong answer moves through diagnosis before reaching for a fix:

1. **Profile first.** Open the framework's devtools profiler, record while scrolling, and check whether the cost is render count, render duration, or something outside rendering entirely (layout thrashing, an expensive computation per row).
2. **Check the row count against what's actually rendered.** If it's a genuinely long list (thousands of rows) and every row exists as a real DOM node regardless of scroll position, virtualization is very likely the fix — render only the visible window instead.
3. **Check for unmemoized expensive work per row.** A `.filter()`, a date-formatting call, or a derived computation re-run from scratch on every parent re-render for every row is a common culprit that memoization (not virtualization) solves.
4. **Check for unstable references defeating existing memoization.** A row wrapped in `React.memo` that still re-renders every time usually means an inline object or callback prop is being recreated each render, silently breaking the shallow-equality check — the same reference-identity issue covered in the hooks topic, here showing up as a performance bug instead of a stale-closure one.

Naming which of these four you'd check, in order, is a far stronger answer than jumping straight to "I'd add virtualization," because half of real jank bugs turn out to be memoization or reference-stability issues instead.
